hints: Notice that the battery drives current in at terminal 1 and out at terminal 2, while terminals 3 and 4 are only joined together outside the box by the right ammeter.
Recall Kirchhoff's current law: two ammeters read the same only if every charge that passes through one must then pass through the other, with no alternative branch or isolated loop.
Compare each box diagram for a single continuous path 1 to 3 to right ammeter to 4 to 2 versus a split at 1 or a loop around 3-4 disconnected from 1-2.
walkthrough: Identify the external connections: left ammeter is in series with terminal 1, terminal 2 returns to the battery, and the right ammeter connects terminal 3 to terminal 4.
State the governing rule: by conservation of charge, ammeters in series carry identical current, while current splits at a junction so a main-line ammeter reads the sum of branch currents.
Test for a single loop: the identical-reading box must connect 1 through to 3, then via the right ammeter to 4, then back to 2, with no extra branch between 1 and 2.
Check option D: 1 is joined to 3 by a resistor and 2 is joined to 4 by a wire, giving the loop battery to 1 to resistor to 3 to right ammeter to 4 to wire to 2 to battery.
In that loop the current $I$ has nowhere else to go, so left-ammeter current equals resistor current equals right-ammeter current.
Options A, B and C all fail this: A leaves the 3-4 loop isolated, B short-circuits 1 to 2 and 3 to 4 with wires, and C provides a direct 1-2 resistor in parallel with the 1-3-4 route.
Therefore the only circuit with both ammeters in series gives identical readings. This is option D.

A.explanation: The 3-4 resistor is in parallel with the ideal right ammeter, so the right loop is isolated from the battery and its ammeter reads near zero while the left ammeter reads the 1-2 resistor current.

B.explanation: Terminals 1, 3, 4 and 2 are all joined by wires that short-circuit the 1-2 resistor, so the left ammeter carries a large short-circuit current and the right ammeter is shorted by the 3-4 wire.

C.explanation: Current entering 1 splits at 1 into a direct 1-2 resistor branch and a 1-3 resistor branch through the right ammeter, so by Kirchhoff's first law the left ammeter reads the sum and is larger.

D.explanation: Terminals 1 to 3 through a resistor and 4 to 2 through a wire place the left ammeter, resistor and right ammeter in one series loop, so the same current $I$ passes through both ammeters.
